p: Copper reacts with chlorine by itself: Cu + Cℓ₂ → CuCℓ₂ is spontaneous. The reverse never happens by itself. But dip two graphite rods into copper(II) chloride solution and connect a battery: copper forms on one rod and chlorine gas bubbles off the other.
**Electrolytic cell:** an electrochemical cell that uses electrical energy to cause a non-spontaneous redox reaction to occur. Thus, electrical energy is converted into chemical energy.

screens.h: The jobs never change; only the signs differ
p: Oxidation is still at the anode and reduction at the cathode, as in every electrochemical cell.
rules: **Anode (+):** the positive terminal pulls electrons out of the anode, so a species there must **give up** electrons: it is oxidised.
**Cathode (−):** the negative terminal pushes electrons into the cathode, so a species there **accepts** them: it is reduced.

screens.q: Three learners discuss the CuCℓ₂ cell.
choices: Aisha: The electrode joined to the positive terminal is the cathode, because the Cu²⁺ ions are positive.
Positive Cu²⁺ ions are attracted to the **negative** electrode, the cathode.
Pieter: The positive electrode is the anode: it attracts the Cℓ⁻ ions and takes their electrons, so Cℓ⁻ is oxidised.
The anode is joined to the positive terminal; anions move to it and are oxidised there.
Lerato: Electrons flow through the solution from the anode to the cathode.
Electrons flow only through the wires and electrodes; **ions** carry the charge through the solution.
screens.why: Pieter ✓. Each electrode is a hand-over point: electrons carry the charge in the wires, ions carry it in the solution, and a half-reaction at each electrode surface links the two.

ask.prompt: Which half-reaction happens at the cathode?
choices: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
The cathode is joined to the negative terminal: Cu²⁺ accepts electrons there and is reduced.
2Cℓ⁻ → Cℓ₂ + 2e⁻
That is an oxidation: it happens at the anode.
Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
Reduction happens at the cathode: the electrons must be on the left.

lines.side: In a concentrated solution the high [Cℓ⁻] makes the oxidation of Cℓ⁻ predominant (29.3).

lines.x: Oxidising agent: Cu²⁺ ✓ (it is reduced). Reducing agent: Cℓ⁻ ✓ (it is oxidised).

ask.prompt: Work out E^{θ}_{cell} for this cell.

traps: Use the electrodes of THIS cell: Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode (+0,34 V) and Cℓ⁻ is oxidised at the anode (+1,36 V), so E^{θ}_{cell} = 0,34 − 1,36. Not the bigger value minus the smaller.

lines.x: Negative, so the reaction is non-spontaneous under standard conditions ✓: the supply must provide more than 1,02 V to drive it.

why: A learner names Cu as the oxidising agent. Explain the mistake.
Cu is the product ✓. The oxidising agent is the reactant that accepts electrons: Cu²⁺ ✓.

p: A solid ionic compound does not conduct: its ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice. **Melt** it and the ions are free to move.
There is no water, so the only species are the ions of the compound: the **cation is reduced** to the metal at the cathode and the **anion is oxidised** at the anode.
Sodium **can** be made this way, because there is no water to compete with Na⁺ at the cathode.

screens.h: In a solution, water joins both contests
p: In a solution there is a second player at **both** electrodes: **water**. Water can be reduced at the cathode (−0,83 V) and oxidised at the anode (+1,23 V). The reaction that wins is the **predominant half-reaction**.
At the cathode the strongest oxidising agent present is reduced; at the anode the strongest reducing agent present is oxidised, and that includes the anode metal itself.

rules: **Below water: the metal forms.** Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Ni²⁺, Cu²⁺ and Ag⁺ are stronger oxidising agents than water, so the metal is deposited on the cathode.
#c92a2a
**Above water: water is reduced.** K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Aℓ³⁺ are weaker, so 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻. Hydrogen bubbles off, and the OH⁻ makes the solution round the cathode basic.
#c92a2a
**Concentration does not change the cathode.** Even a concentrated solution of Aℓ³⁺, Mg²⁺ or Na⁺ gives hydrogen. Concentration matters only at the anode, for Cℓ⁻.
**Only an ANODE can be active.** A metal anode is a reducing agent at the surface: if it is the strongest one present, it is oxidised and dissolves (Cu, +0,34 V, beats I⁻ and H₂O).

screens.q: A learner writes: “Na⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode, so they are reduced to sodium when NaCℓ(aq) is electrolysed.” What forms at the cathode?
choices: Sodium, because Na⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode.
Attraction decides only which way the ions drift; Table 4 decides which species reacts.
Hydrogen, because Na⁺ is a weaker oxidising agent than H₂O.
So **water** is reduced: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻.
Chlorine, because Cℓ⁻ is reduced.
Cℓ⁻ is oxidised, at the anode. At the cathode a species is reduced.
screens.why: Attraction decides only which way the ions drift; Table 4 decides which species reacts. Na⁺ is a weaker oxidising agent than H₂O, so **water** is reduced and H₂ forms. Sodium forms only from **molten** NaCℓ.

screens.h: At the anode: is the anode active? Then concentration
p: SO₄²⁻ and NO₃⁻ are never oxidised at the anode: in Table 4 they appear only on the left, as oxidising agents.
rules: **An active metal anode (Cu, Ni …):** the **anode itself** is oxidised, because it is a stronger reducing agent than water and the anions: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.
**Inert anode + I⁻ or Br⁻:** the **halide** is oxidised (it is a stronger reducing agent than water): 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
**Inert anode + SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻ or F⁻:** **water** is oxidised: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Oxygen bubbles; the solution round the anode becomes acidic.
**Inert anode + Cℓ⁻:** **concentration decides.** Concentrated: Cℓ₂ forms. Dilute: mainly O₂ forms.

screens.h: Three industries, the same two contests
p: **Electroplating:** the **object** is the **cathode** (−); the **anode** (+) is a bar of the **plating metal**; the electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal. The concentration of the metal ions **stays the same**.

**Electrorefining** of copper: impure copper is the anode, pure copper the cathode. Impurities that are stronger reducing agents than Cu (such as Co) dissolve at the anode; only Cu²⁺ is deposited on the cathode.
**The membrane cell:** saturated brine. Anode: 2Cℓ⁻ → Cℓ₂ + 2e⁻. Cathode: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻. Only Na⁺ ions (and water) pass through the membrane; Cℓ⁻ and OH⁻ cannot.

choices: Co is a stronger reducing agent than Cu; Au is a weaker reducing agent than Cu. So Co is oxidised, but Au is not.

Co²⁺ is a weaker oxidising agent than Cu²⁺, so Co is oxidised.
At the anode, compare the species that could be OXIDISED, the reducing agents: “Co is a stronger reducing agent than Cu, so Co is oxidised.”
Gold is less reactive, so it stays in the anode.
“Less reactive” names no agent. Au is a weaker reducing agent than Cu, so it is not oxidised: it falls off as anode sludge.
